lead: Dependency grammar describes a sentence as words joined by labelled links. Each link runs from a head word to a dependent word, and every word except one leans on exactly one other. Dependency parsing is the job of finding the best set of such links for a given sentence and its part-of-speech tags. It exists because many languages, Hindi and Tamil among them, move words around freely while keeping the same word-to-word relations. Question answering, information extraction and machine translation all use dependency trees to find out who did what to whom.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for constituency as a contrast, and the POS tags of Unit 2, because a dependency parser reads tags as well as words.

blocks.text: A dependency tree treats every word as a node. A link runs from a head to a dependent. The head governs the relation; the dependent leans on it. In The boy ate the cake, the verb ate is the head of boy and of cake. Boy is the head of The, and cake is the head of the.
One word has no head inside the sentence. It is joined to a special node called ROOT, placed at position 0 before the first word. Here ate is that word. The links must satisfy four conditions.

items: Each word has exactly one head, except the one word that links to ROOT.
Exactly one word links to ROOT.
No cycles: following heads from any word must end at ROOT.
All words are connected: no word floats free.

blocks.text: Each link carries a label naming the grammatical relation. The table lists the labels used in this chapter.
Label names come from the treebank the parser learned from. Some syllabi call the preposition link prep, others case or obl. The shape of the tree matters more than the spelling of the label.

Draw the arcs above the words. A tree is projective when no two arcs cross. The test is simple: if word i is the head of word j, every word strictly between them must be a descendant of i. An arc that crosses another is a crossing arc, and a tree containing one is non-projective.

English is mostly projective, but questions and fronted phrases break it. Hindi and Tamil usually put the verb last and let arguments appear in several orders. Their bracketing into phrases shifts as words move; the head-dependent links do not. That stability is the reason dependency grammar suits free word order languages: the parser predicts relations, not positions.
So the parser's task is the same everywhere. Score the plausible links, then pick one complete, legal tree.
Arc-standard parsing builds the tree left to right using two lists.

items: Stack: words read from the sentence, with ROOT at the bottom, whose head and dependents are not yet all fixed. A word is popped only when it has been given a head and has taken all its dependents.
Buffer: words not yet read, in sentence order.
Arc set: the links built so far.

blocks.text: Let i be the word on top of the stack and j the first word in the buffer. Four actions are possible.

items: SHIFT: move j from the buffer to the top of the stack.
LEFT-ARC(l): add the arc j → i with label l, then pop i. Allowed only if i has no head yet and i is not ROOT; ROOT is never popped.

RIGHT-ARC(l): add the arc i → j with label l, remove j from the buffer, then pop i and put it back at the front of the buffer so it can take more dependents. Allowed only when j already has all its own dependents.
Stop when the buffer is empty and the stack holds only ROOT.

blocks.text: Which action is right? During training the gold tree answers that. A program called the oracle reads the current configuration and returns the correct move.

A classifier then learns to imitate the oracle. Its features are the top stack words, their POS tags, and the first words of the buffer; its output is a score for each legal action. At test time the parser takes the best-scoring legal action and never backtracks, so one early mistake spoils later arcs.
Graph-based parsing takes the other route. Every possible head-dependent pair is scored on its own, and the tree with the largest total score is found exactly by the Chu-Liu/Edmonds algorithm.

A neural shift-reduce parser replaces hand-written features with embeddings. The top three stack words and the next three buffer words are looked up as vectors and fed to a feed-forward network that scores SHIFT, LEFT-ARC and RIGHT-ARC. Only a few universities go this deep; most exams stop at the four actions above.

examples.question: The gold dependency tree for The boy ate the cake quickly has these arcs: ate → boy (nsubj), boy → The (det), ate → cake (dobj), cake → the (det), ate → quickly (advmod), and ate → ROOT. A system outputs every arc correctly except that it links cake → quickly (advmod) instead of ate → quickly (advmod). Counting every arc, including the one from ate to ROOT, find UAS and LAS.
steps: Count the gold arcs: five word-to-word arcs plus one ROOT arc gives 6 arcs. The denominator for both measures is 6.
Unlabelled attachment: an arc is correct when head and dependent match, whatever the label. Five arcs match. The wrong one has head cake where the gold has ate, so it fails. UAS = 5 / 6 = 0.8333.

Labelled attachment: an arc is correct only when head, dependent and label all match. The same five arcs match. The wrong arc has the wrong head and also carries advmod under the wrong head, so it fails. LAS = 5 / 6 = 0.8333.

The two scores coincide because the single error breaks the head and the label together. If the system had linked ate → quickly with the label dobj, UAS would stay 0.8333 while LAS would fall to 4 / 6 = 0.6667.
examples.answer: There are 6 arcs; 5 are correct, so UAS = 5/6 = 0.8333 and LAS = 5/6 = 0.8333.
examples.check:
gold = [("ate","boy","nsubj"),("boy","The","det"),("ate","cake","dobj"),("cake","the","det"),("ate","quickly","advmod"),("ate","ROOT","root")]
pred = [("ate","boy","nsubj"),("boy","The","det"),("ate","cake","dobj"),("cake","the","det"),("cake","quickly","advmod"),("ate","ROOT","root")]
n = len(gold)
u = sum(1 for g, p in zip(gold, pred) if g[0] == p[0] and g[1] == p[1])
l = sum(1 for g, p in zip(gold, pred) if g == p)
print(n)
print(u)
print(l)
print(round(u / n, 4))
print(round(l / n, 4))

traps: Dropping the ROOT arc from the denominator. The link from the main word to ROOT is an arc and is counted; a six-word sentence with a root arc has 6 arcs, not 5.
Counting words instead of arcs. UAS and LAS are ratios of arcs; a 10-word sentence contributes 10 arcs, not 9 or 10 tokens minus something.
Accepting a set of high-scoring arcs that is not a tree. A word with two heads, or a cycle with no path to ROOT, is invalid and scores nothing, however sensible each arc looks alone.
Reversing arc direction. Arcs run head → dependent, so ate → boy is correct and boy → ate is wrong even though both name the same pair.
Treating a crossing arc as an error. Projectivity is a structural property; free word order languages often need non-projective trees, and a parser that forbids them will be wrong.

quiz.q: Define head and dependent in a dependency tree.
quiz.a: The head is the word that governs a relation; the dependent is the word that attaches to it. The link is written head → dependent, as in ate → boy.

quiz.q: State the four conditions a dependency tree must satisfy.
quiz.a: Every word has exactly one head except the root word; exactly one word links to ROOT; there are no cycles; all words are connected.

quiz.q: Why does dependency grammar suit Hindi and Tamil better than a strict phrase-structure grammar?
quiz.a: Those languages allow arguments in several orders with the verb usually last, so phrase bracketing changes from one order to another. The head-dependent links stay the same, so the parser predicts relations rather than positions.

quiz.q: What is the difference between LEFT-ARC and RIGHT-ARC in arc-standard parsing?
quiz.a: LEFT-ARC makes the first buffer word the head of the stack top and pops the stack top. RIGHT-ARC makes the stack top the head of the first buffer word, removes that buffer word, and moves the stack top back to the front of the buffer.

quiz.q: Configuration: stack = [ROOT, boy], buffer = [ate, the, cake], and the gold tree has ate → boy (nsubj). Which action applies and what is the new configuration?
quiz.a: The head ate is in the buffer and the dependent boy is on top of the stack, so it is LEFT-ARC(nsubj). Add ate → boy (nsubj), pop boy: stack = [ROOT], buffer = [ate, the, cake].

quiz.q: A gold tree has 5 arcs including the ROOT arc. A system gets 4 arcs right unlabelled, and 3 of those also carry the right label. Find UAS and LAS.
A parser outputs cake → quickly (advmod) and ate → quickly (advmod). Explain what goes wrong and how it affects UAS and LAS.
quiz.a: The output is not a tree because quickly has two heads, so it is invalid as a whole. If it is scored arc by arc anyway, the spurious arc cake → quickly is ignored: UAS and LAS divide correct arcs by the 6 gold arcs, giving 5/6 = 0.8333, so the spurious arc does not lower the score. Repair the output to one valid tree before scoring.

quiz.q: Two arcs (2 → 5) and (4 → 1) appear in a tree. Say whether the tree is projective and justify your answer.
quiz.a: They cross: 2 → 5 spans positions 3 and 4, and 4 → 1 spans positions 2 and 3, so each arc has an endpoint strictly inside the other's span. The tree is non-projective.

beyond: Not for the exam. Universal Dependencies is the treebank family that standardised dependency labels across dozens of languages, including several Indian ones. It uses obj rather than dobj, and case/obl rather than prep. Open-source libraries such as spaCy and Stanza ship pretrained dependency parsers, so a project can get trees in a few lines of Python. Research now leans on graph-based and neural parsers, and on parsing that feeds semantic roles and AMR graphs downstream. Worth searching next: Universal Dependencies, transition-based versus graph-based parsing, and cross-lingual dependency parsing for Indian languages.
